title: Docs Context Layer
eyebrow: Proposal · where the restructure stands, and folding Trail-Code's job into the docs

short.lead: The restructure (issue #306, "restructure into a shared core with project boundaries and six optional sub-plugins") has finished its first step only. The 2.68.1 patch passed your QA on 2026-10-16, but its five issues (#307 to #311) are still open, waiting for you to close them. The next step, a grilling session on the 28 places where the rules contradict each other, has not started, and no build sub-issues exist yet. Since then the work has gone to side fixes: the credit check (#315, merged) and six new loop issues (#322 to #327). That pause makes this the right moment to change course. Trail-Code (trailhq/Trail-Code, MIT licence, runs locally) does what our docs were meant to do: a session reads a map instead of searching code. This page proposes making the Docs part of the restructure the default instead of an option, with every doc naming what it depends on and what depends on it, kept current automatically.
short.hint: Tap a row to see what it covers.
items: Every repo already has landing, roadmap, state, systems, today and decisions folders, and the docstiers hook checks that they exist. The tier-4 system docs say what each system owns and what it does not own, and cite code to file:line. These are close to Trail-Code's map, but the dependencies are written as prose, not as a list a tool can read.

The archivist moves long code comments into the system docs and leaves a doc-ref pointer behind. docref.py checks that each pointer still resolves. This is a link from code to doc in one direction. Nothing yet links a doc back to the files it describes, so nothing can tell when a doc has gone stale.
Reused; the reverse link is new.

docs/6-decisions/Decisions.md records what was decided, what was ruled out and why. That is Trail-Code's "decisions" learnings under another name. Trail-Code adds one thing we lack: before a commit, it checks the change against past decisions and quotes the one it contradicts.
Reused; the pre-commit check is new.
A code map and a lookup-first habit

Nothing tells a session to read the docs before searching code, and there is no who-calls-what map. Trail-Code builds one with tree-sitter (a parser library), on this machine, with no model and no network, and its hooks put the matching files and functions into each prompt. Its README claims 46% fewer tool calls across 162 runs. I have not run it, so that figure is theirs, not measured here.
Today a doc changes only when a session remembers. Nothing notices that a file a doc describes was edited, and nothing lists which docs need updating after a change.

changes: chg
The restructure plan (issue #306)
Docs moves from an optional part to the core, and gains the context layer.
Docs is one of four optional sub-plugins, holding the doc tiers, the long-comment harvest, doc-ref pointers and the archivist.
Docs is installed by default. It adds a dependency header on every doc, a staleness check, a lookup-first prompt hook and a decisions check before commits.
The grilling session on the 28 rule contradictions still comes first, as #306 says. This change is added to its list so it is settled in the same pass.
new
A dependency header on every doc
Each doc opens with the same four lines: what it covers, what it depends on, what depends on it, and when it was last checked against the code.

covers names the source files and functions. depends-on and depended-on-by name other docs and systems. The project-docs skill's templates gain the header, and docstiers refuses a tier-4 doc without one. A fixed shape means a person or an agent always knows which line to read.
new
A staleness check after every change
When a turn edits a file that a doc's covers line names, the end-of-reply check names that doc as owed an update.

It compares each edited path against every doc's covers line. A doc owed an update is listed once per turn, with the depended-on-by list so the knock-on docs are named too. It reports and does not block, like the commit check.
new
A lookup-first prompt hook
Each prompt gets a short list of the docs whose covers line matches the files or systems it mentions.
The list is drawn from the dependency headers, so it costs a few hundred characters, not a code search. With the code map from the first choice, it can also name functions and their callers.
new
A decisions check before commit
Before a commit, the change is compared against decisions that name the same files, and a contradiction is quoted.

Decisions.md entries gain a touches line naming files. The guard hook that already runs on git commit adds the comparison. A clash asks for a reason in the commit message; it does not refuse the commit.
choices: map
Where should the who-calls-what code map come from?
A
Install Trail-Code for its code map only, and keep our own docs as the record of decisions

Local open-source code does the parsing in 23 languages, Python included. We write only the dependency headers and the hooks. Costs: it needs Node (installed here), it adds its own hooks to .claude, and its anonymous usage ping must be turned off with DO_NOT_TRACK=1.
B
Install all of Trail-Code, learnings included, and retire the decisions log
Least to build. Two problems: its learnings live in .trail/, a second place beside our six tiers, and its team features are marked "soon".
C
Build our own map in Python with the standard ast module, no Trail-Code
No new dependency. It only maps Python files, so Unity C# and web projects get no map, and it rebuilds what Trail-Code already does.

The house rule "Open source first" puts local open-source tools at the top, which favours A or B. Any choice still gets a trial on this repo, measuring tool calls with and without it, before it ships.
auto
How should docs be kept current?
A
The end-of-reply check names each doc owed an update, and the session writes it
The session already holds the change in context, so the update is cheap. It reports and does not block.
B
The same check, but it blocks the reply until the doc is updated
Docs never fall behind. It adds another blocking check, and blocking checks caused the loops in #303 and #322.
C
A helper agent updates the docs in the background after each change
Nothing for the session to do. It costs a helper run per change and needs the two-helper limit.
In all three, the dependency headers are what tells the check which docs a change touches.
when
When should this be built?
A
Add it to #306 and settle it in the grilling session, then build it inside the Docs part of the restructure
One build, in the new structure. Nothing is built twice in today's 8,365-line hook.py.
B
Build the dependency headers and the staleness check now, in today's plugin, before the restructure
You get the benefit sooner. The code moves again when the restructure splits hook.py.
Either way, the five 2.68.1 issues (#307 to #311) should close first, since their QA has passed.

wrapup.summary: The restructure stopped after the 2.68.1 patch. This proposes making the Docs part a default context layer, using Trail-Code's ideas and possibly its code map.
wrapup.changing: Nothing yet. If approved: the plan in #306, the project-docs templates, and four new checks in the Docs part.
wrapup.blocking: Your answers to the three choices, and whether to close #307 to #311.
wrapup.next: I update #306 and its systems doc, open one issue per new check, and trial Trail-Code's map on this repo if you pick A for the code map.
